title: How to Get a Liquor License in Texas
summary: Opening a liquor store in Texas? Learn which TABC permit you need (P, BQ, or BF), what it costs, who qualifies, and each step of the application.
body_markdown:
To open a liquor store in Texas, you need a permit from the Texas Alcoholic Beverage Commission (TABC), but the type of permit you require depends on the exact beverages you’re selling.


The good news for new owners is that Texas doesn't cap licenses by population the way California and Florida do. There's no lottery and no private market where licenses sell for six figures. You apply for a new permit, pay a state fee in the low thousands, and wait for TABC to review your application.


## Which Liquor License Do You Need to Open a Liquor Store in Texas?


Texas doesn't issue a single "liquor license." TABC issues licenses and permits by business type, and the one you need depends on what you plan to sell. A liquor store sells off-premise, meaning customers buy sealed containers and drink them somewhere else.


There are four off-premise options for a retail store:


- **Package Store Permit (P):** Lets you sell distilled spirits, wine, and malt beverages (beer and ale) in sealed containers. This is the permit for a full-line liquor store.
- **Wine-Only Package Store Permit (Q):** Built for wine shops that don't sell spirits. It covers wine and malt beverages.
- **Wine and Malt Beverage Retailer's Off-Premise Permit (BQ):** Covers beer and wine, but not spirits. Convenience stores, grocery stores, and beer-and-wine shops typically hold this one.
- **Retail Dealer's Off-Premise License (BF):** For beer-only establishments.


The P permit covers more than over-the-counter sales. It already includes the right to host product tastings in the store and to deliver orders to customers within the city limits or a 2-mile radius, as long as the delivery address is in a wet area for that product. If you want to sell to other retailers, such as bars and restaurants, you’ll need to add a Local Distributor’s Permit (LP).


The P permit also comes with a physical requirement that surprises some first-time owners. The store has to be completely separated from any other business by a solid floor-to-ceiling wall, with no connecting doors, shared restrooms, or shared entry.


That's why you see Texas grocery chains run their liquor stores as a separate storefront next door instead of an aisle inside.


## Can You Apply for a New Liquor License in Texas, or Do You Have to Buy One?


In Texas, you need to apply for a new liquor license. The state doesn't limit how many package store permits can exist in a city or county, so there's no waiting for a population-based opening.


That's a major difference from quota states. New off-sale[general licenses in California](https://www.santehq.com/blog/blog-california-liquor-license-for-liquor-stores) , for instance, are released once a year through a drawing, and most new owners end up buying an existing license from a current holder, often for far more than the state fee. Texas owners skip that step entirely.


The flip side is that Texas permits can’t be transferred. If you buy an existing liquor store’s assets, the seller’s permit doesn’t come with it. You’ll need to apply for your own permit in your own name, and you can’t legally sell alcohol at that location until it’s issued. Buying the company that holds the permit works differently: the permit stays with that company, and the ownership change has to be reported to TABC within 30 days.


Talk to TABC or a licensing attorney before you structure the deal.


## Who Is Eligible for a Liquor License in Texas?


TABC reviews every owner listed on the application, not only the person who signs it. To qualify, applicants generally need to meet these conditions:


- Be at least 21 years old.
- Have finished any felony sentence at least five years before applying, and have no violations of the Alcoholic Beverage Code or TABC rules involving moral turpitude in the six months before applying.
- Stay within one tier of the industry. Texas follows the three-tier system, which separates manufacturers, distributors, and retailers. As a retailer, you can't hold an interest in a brewery, distillery, or distributor permit.
- Disclose every owner and funding source. Hidden owners or money you can't account for are among the fastest ways to stall an application.


Texas also limits who can own a package store. Two ownership rules apply specifically to P permits:


- **Public corporations can't hold package store permits.** Under Alcoholic Beverage Code §22.16, a company listed on a stock exchange, or one with more than 35 owners, is barred from holding a P permit. The only exceptions are package stores located in hotels and public companies that already held package store permits in April 1995 (only two qualified as of 2022 court filings), which is why Walmart and Costco sell beer and wine in Texas but not spirits.
- **No one can hold an interest in more than 250 package stores** (§22.04).


## Where Can You Open a Liquor Store in Texas?


In Texas, the address can decide whether you get a permit at all. Confirm three things first:


- **Wet/dry status:** Local option elections decide what can be sold where. Some areas allow beer and wine but not spirits, which rules out a P permit. Check the exact address with TABC, since a city can vote differently from its county.
- **Distance rules:** Cities and counties can ban sales within 300 feet of a church, school, or public hospital, or within 1,000 feet of a school at the school's request (§109.33). Church and hospital distances are measured door to door along the street. School distances run in a straight line from property line to property line.
- **Zoning:** Confirm with the planning department that a package store is allowed at the address. TABC needs the city or county to certify the location before it will process your application.


## How Much Does a Liquor License Cost in Texas?


For most new liquor stores, the permit itself costs a few thousand dollars over two years. That puts Texas at the low end of[liquor license costs](https://www.santehq.com/blog/how-much-does-a-liquor-license-cost) nationally, since you're paying state fees rather than a market price for a scarce license.


Here's what to budget for:


Cost Amount What to know


TABC permit fee $1,800 (P), $1,900 (BQ), $1,100 (BF) Covers two years. Add-on permits like the Local Distributor’s Permit (LP, $1,300) have their own fees.


Local fees Up to $500 for a P permit; up to $60 for BQ or BF Capped at half of the permit’s old statutory fee, not half of the current TABC fee. Since September 2025 (SB 1008), cities and counties can’t charge this fee to food establishments that already pay a food operating fee. That mainly helps grocery and convenience stores; a standalone liquor store without a food permit will usually still pay it.


Conduct surety bond $5,000, or $10,000 within 1,000 feet of a public school You pay an annual premium to a bonding company, usually a small percentage of the bond. TABC also accepts a letter of credit or a certificate of deposit.


Business setup $300 to form an LLC or corporation Paid to the Texas Secretary of State, plus a small fee if you file an assumed name.


Professional help (optional) Several thousand dollars Many owners with straightforward off-premise applications file on their own.


The permit is only a small slice of your startup budget. Inventory, rent, fixtures, coolers, and your POS system make up most of the[cost of opening a liquor store](https://www.santehq.com/blog/how-much-does-it-cost-to-open-a-liquor-store) , which often runs into the hundreds of thousands of dollars before you sell your first bottle.


## How to Apply for a Liquor License in Texas


### Step 1: Choose your permit and confirm your location


Decide what you'll sell, then run the location checks above: wet/dry status, distance rules, and zoning. Doing this before you sign a lease is the single best way to avoid losing months and money on an address that can't be permitted.


When you look at floor plans, keep the P permit's layout rules in mind. You'll need a separate store with its own front entrance, a rear or side door for deliveries or emergency exit, and an ADA-compliant restroom.


### Step 2: Get local approval


Most permit applications need the city and county to certify that the location complies with local rules before TABC will move forward. Depending on where you are, that can involve the city secretary, the county clerk, or the county tax assessor-collector.


### Step 3: Set up your business


TABC needs to know exactly who owns the business that will hold the permit, so set it up before you apply by:


- **Forming your entity** (LLC, corporation, or partnership) with the Texas Secretary of State, and filing an assumed name if you'll operate under a different store name.
- **Getting an EIN** from the IRS.
- **Getting a sales tax permit** from the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts. Off-premise alcohol sales are subject to state and local sales tax, so you'll need to set up your[liquor store sales tax compliance](https://www.santehq.com/blog/off-premise-retail-tax-laws-for-liquor-stores) correctly from your first sale.
- **Registering with the TTB** using Form 5630.5d. Every retailer that sells alcohol must register with the federal Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau before it starts selling.


### Step 4: Gather your documents


Expect to provide:


- Personal information for every owner, officer, and manager, for background checks
- Your entity documents and ownership structure
- Your lease, deed, or other proof that you can use the property
- The local certification from Step 2
- A publisher’s affidavit showing you published notice of your application in a local newspaper (see Step 6)
- Your certification from the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
- Your conduct surety bond
- Any notices or affidavits required for your permit type and location


Incomplete applications are the most common reason for delays, so check the list against TABC's current requirements for your permit before you file.


### Step 5: Apply through AIMS and pay the fees


TABC takes applications through AIMS, its Alcohol Industry Management System. You'll create an account, complete the application for your permit type, upload your documents, and pay the state fee. AIMS is also where TABC will ask for corrections and where you can check your status.


### Step 6: Complete any notice requirements


You may have heard that Texas applicants must post a sign on the property for 60 days before a permit is issued. That rule only applies to on-premise businesses like bars and restaurants – P, BQ, and BF applicants don't have to post it.


Other notices still apply, though. P, BQ, and BF applicants must publish notice of their application, at their own cost, in two consecutive issues of a local newspaper. The notice lists the permit type, the store’s address, and the owners’ names (plus officers’ names and titles for a corporation). You’ll submit the publisher’s affidavit with your application.


If your store will be near a school, you may also have to notify school officials in writing before you file. Ask your TABC office which other notices apply to your permit and location.


### Step 7: Respond to TABC's review


TABC reviews your application, runs background checks, and may contact you for missing information. For off-premise permits like P, BQ, and BF, only government officials can file a protest. That includes the mayor, city council members, county officials, the police chief, and the district attorney. A protest can lead to a hearing before TABC decides on your permit.


Neighbors can't protest these permits directly, though they can take their concerns to their local officials.


### Step 8: Receive your permit and open


Once TABC approves the application, it issues the permit. Display it where customers can see it, and don't sell alcohol until it's in hand.


## How Long Does It Take to Get a Liquor License in Texas?


TABC’s average processing time dropped to about 26 days in fiscal 2024, and its own guidance tells applicants to expect roughly 30 to 35 days from the date they submit a complete application.. Applications that need corrections, draw a protest, or wait on local certification can take longer.


However, the TABC review is only part of the timeline. Finding a location that passes the wet/dry, distance, and zoning checks, setting up your business, and getting local sign-off should all happen before you file. A realistic plan is to start four to six months before your target opening date.


## Why Liquor License Applications Get Delayed or Denied in Texas


TABC’s processing times assume a complete, problem-free application, but there are issues that could slow an application down or lead to a denial:


- **Missing or inconsistent paperwork:** A missing document or an ownership detail that doesn't match across forms sends the application back to you.
- **Undisclosed owners or unclear funding:** TABC wants to see everyone with a financial interest. Leaving someone off is treated seriously.
- **A disqualifying background:** A recent felony or moral turpitude violation by any listed owner can sink the application.
- **The wrong area:** A dry or beer-and-wine-only area can't support a P permit, no matter how complete the application is.
- **Distance or zoning problems:** A location inside a local distance limit, or zoned for a different use, won't get local certification.
- **A tied interest:** Any ownership link to a manufacturer or distributor conflicts with the three-tier rules.
- **Protests:** Local officials, such as the mayor, police chief, or district attorney, can protest an off-premise application, which can lead to a hearing and add months to the licensing process.
- **Selling before official approval:** Selling before your permit is issued, including under a previous owner's permit after you buy a store, can cost you the application.


## What Happens After You Get Your Texas Liquor License?


Finally getting your permit is a good start, but TABC can fine you, suspend your permit, or cancel it for various violations along the way. The following rules can lower those risks:


### Follow package store hours


Texas package stores can sell from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m., Monday through Saturday. They must stay closed on Sundays, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, and New Year's Day. When Christmas or New Year's Day falls on a Sunday, package stores also close the following Monday.


These rules apply to the whole business, so you can't keep the doors open on a Sunday to sell mixers or snacks.


Beer and wine follow different hours. BQ and BF holders can sell from 7 a.m. to midnight on weekdays, until 1 a.m. on Saturday night, and from 10 a.m. on Sundays.


### Pay distributors on the right terms


Texas sets payment rules between retailers and wholesalers.


Beer purchases fall under the cash law, for example, so you pay on delivery. Spirits and wine purchases, however, fall under the credit law, which gives you a limited window to pay.


Falling behind on your payments can put you on a delinquent list and cut off your ability to buy.


### Renew every two years


Texas permits run for two years. Put the expiration date on your calendar well ahead of time, and keep your sales tax filings current, since unresolved tax issues can hold up a renewal.


### Post the required signs


Display your permit where customers can see it and post the TABC complaint sign near the door or register. BQ and BF holders must also post a sign saying that drinking on the premises is prohibited, along with the human trafficking sign.


### Train your staff


Texas law doesn't require seller-server certification, but it's worth requiring for every employee. If your staff and their managers are certified within 30 days of hire, you have written alcohol service policies, and you meet TABC's other conditions, your permit is protected under "safe harbor" if an employee sells to a minor.


Without it, the violation counts against your permit.


### Keep clean records and expect inspections


TABC agents can inspect your store during business hours without notice. They'll check that your permit is current and posted, that your inventory traces back to invoices from licensed wholesalers and distributors, and that your staff checks IDs.


Going through a[liquor store inspection checklist](https://www.santehq.com/blog/liquor-store-inspection-checklist) ahead of time means you won’t be scrambling when an agent walks in.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Can you buy an existing liquor license in Texas?


No, Texas licenses and permits can’t be transferred. If you buy an existing liquor store’s assets, you have to apply for your own permit, and you can’t sell alcohol at the location until TABC issues it.


If you buy the company that holds the permit instead, the permit stays with that company and the ownership change must be reported to TABC, so check with TABC or a licensing attorney first.


### How long does a Texas liquor license last?


The Texas liquor license lasts two years from the date it's issued and you’ll need to renew and pay the fee again every two years.


### Can a liquor store with a P permit sell beer and wine?


Yes. A Package Store Permit covers distilled spirits, wine, and malt beverages, so a P permit holder can stock all three.


### Can Texas liquor stores open on Sunday?


No. Package stores must close on Sundays, as well as on Thanksgiving, Christmas Day, and New Year's Day. Grocery and convenience stores with beer-and-wine permits can sell on Sundays starting at 10 a.m.


### Can a Texas liquor store deliver?


Yes. A Package Store Permit (P) already includes delivery to customers within the city limits or a 2-mile radius, as long as the delivery address is in a wet area for that product. Third-party delivery services operate under their own TABC permits. Delivery drivers still have to verify the customer’s age at the door.


### Do you have to be a Texas resident to own a liquor store in Texas?


Courts have struck down durational residency requirements for alcohol retailers, including the U.S. Supreme Court in its 2019 decision in *Tennessee Wine and Spirits Retailers Association v. Thomas* . Ownership rules still apply, though, including the ban on public corporations holding package store permits.


Confirm your situation with TABC before you apply.


### How does the Texas liquor license cost compare to California?


California’s state fees run much higher. A new Type 21 license costs $19,840 to apply plus $1,009 a year, and because licenses are capped by population, many owners end up buying an existing one on the private market for far more.


In Texas, you pay the TABC fee, local fees, and a bond premium, and that’s usually the extent of it.


### Do I need a lawyer to get a liquor license in Texas?


You don’t need a lawyer to get a liquor license in Texas – many owners of off-premise stores file on their own through AIMS. A licensing attorney or consultant is worth considering, however, if your ownership structure is complex, your location is close to a school or church, or you expect a protest.


### Can I get a liquor license in Texas with a criminal record?


It depends on the offense and when it happened. TABC can refuse a permit if fewer than five years have passed since you finished serving a felony sentence, or if you violated the Alcoholic Beverage Code or TABC rules in a way involving moral turpitude in the past six months.


Older or lesser offenses don't automatically rule you out, but disclose everything. Leaving something off the application can be a reason for denial on its own.
